title: Finish dinner three hours before bed
body: When you lie down soon after a meal, stomach acid can flow back up into the food pipe. This is one of the commonest reasons for night-time heartburn and a sour taste in the morning.
try: If you sleep at 11 pm, aim to finish dinner by 8 pm. Keep late-night snacks light.

title: Sugary drinks feed fatty liver
body: Soft drinks, packaged juices and sweetened tea or coffee deliver a large dose of sugar that the liver turns into fat. Regular sugary drinks are closely linked with fatty liver, even in people who are not overweight.
try: Swap one sugary drink a day for plain water, unsweetened chaas or nimbu pani without sugar.

title: Most of us eat too little fibre
body: Adults need about 25 to 30 grams of fibre a day for regular, comfortable bowels. Diets built on white rice, maida and packaged foods usually fall well short.
try: Add one high-fibre food today: a bowl of sprouts, whole dal, a fruit with its peel, or atta with the chokar left in. Increase slowly and drink more water.

title: Tea or coffee on an empty stomach
body: For people prone to acidity, strong tea or coffee as the very first thing in the morning can trigger burning and nausea.
try: Eat something small first, such as a fruit, a few soaked almonds or a roti, then have your tea.

title: ORS comes first in loose motions
body: The main danger of diarrhoea is losing water and salts, not the infection itself. ORS replaces both better than plain water, juice or soft drinks.
try: Keep a few ORS packets at home. If you have none, mix 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water. See a doctor if there is blood, high fever or very little urine.

title: Detox and herbal products can harm the liver
body: Some unregulated herbal powders, weight-loss products, body-building supplements and 'liver tonics' can cause serious liver injury. Natural does not always mean safe.
try: Tell your doctor about every supplement, powder or home remedy you take, including the ones you think are harmless.

title: Why healthy foods can cause gas
body: Rajma, chana, onion, garlic, cabbage and cauliflower contain carbohydrates that gut bacteria ferment. In people with a sensitive gut, this causes bloating and gas.
try: Soak legumes overnight, discard the water and pressure-cook well. Eat smaller portions rather than cutting these foods out completely.

title: Jaundice from water: hepatitis A and E
body: Hepatitis A and E spread through contaminated water and food, and they are a common cause of jaundice in India, especially after the monsoon.
try: Drink boiled or properly filtered water. Avoid cut fruit and pani puri water from roadside stalls. Ask your doctor about the hepatitis A vaccine for children.

title: Spicy food does not cause ulcers
body: Most stomach ulcers are caused by the H. pylori infection or by painkillers. Spicy food can worsen burning in someone who already has gastritis, but it does not create an ulcer.
try: If you have upper stomach pain that keeps coming back, ask about an H. pylori test instead of only avoiding chillies.

title: Small weight loss, big liver benefit
body: Losing 7 to 10 percent of your body weight can reduce liver fat and even reverse early scarring. For a person weighing 80 kg, that is 6 to 8 kg.
try: Aim for a steady loss of half to one kilo a week through smaller portions and daily walking. Crash diets are not needed.

title: How to take isabgol correctly
body: Isabgol (psyllium husk) is a safe fibre supplement for constipation, but it needs enough water to work. Taken with too little water, it can make constipation worse.
try: Start with one teaspoon stirred into a full glass of water, drink it straight away, then drink another glass of water.

title: Milk, curd and bloating
body: Many Indian adults digest milk sugar (lactose) less well as they age, which causes gas and loose stools after milk. Curd, buttermilk and paneer contain much less lactose and are usually better tolerated.
try: If milk bloats you, try a smaller cup taken with a meal, or switch to curd or chaas.

title: There is no liver-friendly alcohol
body: Every type of alcohol, including wine and beer, adds load to the liver. For people with fatty liver, hepatitis B or C, or cirrhosis, even small regular amounts speed up damage.
try: If you have any liver condition, the safest amount of alcohol is none.

title: Painkillers and your stomach
body: Common painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can cause stomach ulcers and bleeding, especially in older people and when taken often.
try: Take them only when needed, after food, for the shortest time. Ask your doctor for a gentler option if you need pain relief regularly.

title: Use your morning reflex
body: Eating breakfast naturally triggers the bowel to move. Ignoring that urge repeatedly is a common cause of constipation.
try: Sit on the toilet for 5 to 10 minutes after breakfast, without your phone. Resting your feet on a small stool to raise your knees makes passing stool easier.

title: Swap maida for whole grains
body: White bread, biscuits, noodles and other maida products have had most of their fibre removed. They digest fast and do little for your bowels or blood sugar.
try: Choose whole-wheat roti, brown or hand-pounded rice, oats, millets like bajra and ragi, and keep the chokar in your atta.

title: Raise the head of your bed
body: For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed by 6 to 8 inches helps gravity keep acid down. Extra pillows only bend the neck and do not work as well.
try: Place bricks or wooden blocks under the legs at the head end of your bed.

title: Coffee and the liver
body: Regular coffee drinkers have a lower risk of liver scarring in many large studies. The benefit is linked to plain coffee, not sugary coffee drinks.
try: If you enjoy coffee, one or two cups a day with little or no sugar is fine for most people with fatty liver.

title: Black stools: what is harmless and what is not
body: Iron tablets and some foods can make stools dark, which is harmless. Stools that are black, sticky and tar-like, especially with weakness or dizziness, can mean bleeding in the stomach.
try: Tar-like black stools with weakness need care the same day. If you are on iron tablets and feel well, mention it at your next visit.

title: Crash diets can cause gallstones
body: Losing weight very fast, or skipping meals for long periods, changes bile and raises the chance of gallstones forming.
try: Lose weight steadily and eat regular, moderate meals rather than long fasts followed by heavy ones.

title: Breaking a fast gently
body: After a long fast, a large fried or very sweet meal can trigger acidity, bloating, and in people with gallstones, a painful attack.
try: Break a fast with water, fruit or a light dish first, and have the main meal a little later.

title: Diabetes and fatty liver go together
body: More than half of people with type 2 diabetes have fatty liver, and they are more likely to develop liver scarring.
try: If you have diabetes, ask your doctor whether your liver has been checked with a blood test and a liver stiffness test.

title: Blood in the stool is not always piles
body: Piles are common, but bleeding can also come from a fissure, polyps, inflammation or, less often, colon cancer, which is increasingly seen in younger adults.
try: Get any rectal bleeding checked once, at any age, especially if it comes with a change in bowel habit or tiredness.

title: Water and constipation
body: Fibre absorbs water to keep stools soft. Without enough fluid, more fibre can actually make stools harder.
try: Drink enough through the day to keep your urine pale yellow, and a little more in hot weather or when you increase fibre.

title: Eating after pancreatitis
body: After an attack of pancreatitis, small low-fat meals are easier on the pancreas while it recovers. Alcohol and smoking both raise the chance of another attack.
try: Choose steamed, boiled or lightly cooked food over fried food, and stop alcohol and smoking completely.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine is for adults too
body: Hepatitis B can cause lifelong liver disease, and adults who were not vaccinated as children are still at risk. The vaccine is safe and given as three doses.
try: Check whether you have had the hepatitis B vaccine. If not, or if you are unsure, ask your doctor about a blood test and vaccination.

title: Festive sweets and food safety
body: Milk-based sweets spoil quickly, and stomach infections rise during the festive season.
try: Buy sweets fresh from a reliable shop, keep them refrigerated, and throw away anything that smells or tastes sour.

title: Festive meals without the acidity
body: Fried snacks, sweets and late dinners together are a common recipe for heartburn during festivals.
try: Have the heavier meal earlier in the day, eat slowly, and take a short walk afterwards instead of lying down.

title: A short walk after meals
body: A gentle 10 to 15 minute walk after eating helps the stomach empty and lowers the rise in blood sugar after the meal.
try: Walk after lunch or dinner today. Keep it gentle; strenuous exercise right after eating can cause cramps.

title: Smoking harms the whole gut
body: Smoking worsens reflux, slows ulcer healing, makes Crohn's disease more severe, and raises the risk of cancers of the food pipe, stomach, pancreas and colon.
try: If you smoke, quitting is one of the best things you can do for your digestion. Ask your doctor about help to stop.
